assembler.title: The Assembler
texts: Day 3. I am done placing casings by hand. Set the multiblock controller down, use the $(item)Structure Assembler$() on it, and it builds every missing block, bottom-up, from casings in my inventory (free in creative).

Lesson learned: $(thing)sneak-use$() first for a dry run. Sparks mark the gaps, and I get a shopping list that counts what I already carry.$(br2)The assembler never breaks blocks - anything in the way is marked, for me to clear myself. It never places $(item)Interface Ports$() automatically either; I swap those in where I want them.
Week two. The big machines are not single blocks but assemblies of $(thing)functional components$(), each with its own crafting chain. Like a real accelerator hall: nothing works alone.

The parts list reads like a CERN inventory: magnets, RF cavities, beam pipes, cryogenics, vacuum pumps, detectors, injectors, lenses, anchors, stabilisers and more. In reality, dipole magnets bend a beam, RF cavities kick it faster, and cryogenics keep superconductors below their critical temperature.

$(thing)Coils$() come in five tiers: Superconducting, Chronosteel, Spacetime Alloy, Cosmic Neutronium and Transfinite. Like a chain and its weakest link, a structure counts only its $(thing)lowest$() coil. Each tier above the first adds 25% speed, and some recipes need a minimum tier (JEI shows it).

$(thing)Field Emitters$() come in three tiers. The lowest emitter tier multiplies how many parallels the tuning panel allows.$(br2)The $(item)Structure Assembler$() places the best tier I carry; in creative, hold the tier you want in your off-hand. Mixing tiers works, but only the lowest counts - I checked twice.
Incident log. A multiblock whose containment reaches zero does not simply stop. What it was holding gets out - and what gets out depends on the machine. I have catalogued five kinds.

$(li)$(thing)Reality Destabilisation$() (colliders, reactors, forges, crucibles): a blast, and the surrounding world starts to come apart. Blocks become $(thing)Fractured Reality$(): they fade in and out and split into smaller copies of themselves, spreading slowly before reality heals.

Anything alive suffers too. Creatures caught in Fractured Reality glitch and splinter like the shadows of higher-dimensional bodies, hit harder and move faster. Villagers and zombies become $(thing)Destabilised Husks$(). I learned that one at a cost.

$(li)$(thing)Spatial$() (singularities, wormholes, universe forging): a $(thing)rupture$() grows for ten seconds, drags everything in, eats the terrain and detonates. $(thing)Void Wraiths$() - tiny living black and white holes - crawl out, and burst like a creeper when they collapse. Hawking would have been delighted. I was not.

$(li)$(thing)Infectious$() (Matrioshka Brain, Reality Compiler, Assembly Line): flying $(thing)Nanite Swarms$() escape. They split when destroyed, down to single units, and any creature that dies infected bursts into a new swarm. Grey goo, in other words - the old nanotech nightmare, given wings.

$(li)$(thing)Temporal$() (Causality Loop Engine): $(thing)Paradox Echoes$() - walking clockwork, one for every player nearby - that rewind themselves when hurt.$(li)$(thing)Dimensional$() (Rift, Tesseract, Breach, Omnilex): a rupture plus $(thing)Law Wraiths$(), broken laws of nature shaped like tesseracts.

Note to self: overclocked machines fail harder. Keep containment up with a $(item)Field Calibrator$(), or install an $(item)Autonomous Calibrator$().$(br2)For server owners: the consequences or the block damage can be disabled in the config, and block damage also respects the $(thing)mobGriefing$() game rule.

Day 1. Science starts with looking. I use a $(item)Spectral Analyzer$() on unusual blocks (beacons, end portal frames, amethyst, sculk, Cherenkov ore...), on Endermen and Wardens, and on $(thing)running$() Theoretical Sciences machines.

Every $(thing)new$() observation grants $(thing)Insight$(). Sneak-use the analyzer to observe the sky of the dimension you are in - splitting starlight into a spectrum is how astronomers first learned what stars are made of.$(br2)Multiblocks are worth the most. A running machine, it turns out, is the best teacher.
Housekeeping. All my machines use standard $(thing)FE$() and expose items, fluids and energy on every side, so any pipe, cable or storage mod works. Inputs can be inserted; outputs can be extracted.

Fluids move the same way: pipes, AE2 import/export buses, storage buses and pattern providers can all fill input tanks and drain output tanks.$(br2)Multiblocks talk to the outside world through $(item)Interface Ports$() placed in the marked positions - and one port is enough for items, fluids and energy alike.

Working by hand: right-click a machine with a bucket or a $(item)Containment Cell$(), or click a tank in its screen while holding one. Containment Cells are proper fluid containers, so tanks, pipes and AE2 can fill and empty them too. Good - some of what I bottle should never touch a bucket.
Day 2. I set up a $(item)Research Terminal$() to keep my thinking in order: it opens the research tree. Each node costs Insight and sometimes materials, and needs its prerequisites.

Machines refuse to run recipes I have not researched - a machine checks the research of whoever placed it.$(br2)For pack makers: this can be turned off in the config, entries can be edited in $(thing)data/*/ts_research$(), and research can be granted with $(thing)/theoreticalsciences research grant$().
Handy trick: sneak-use this Codex to open the research tree from anywhere. I no longer walk back to the terminal every time an idea strikes.

tuning.title: Tuning Notes
texts: Multiblocks are not set-and-forget. Each has a $(thing)tuning panel$() beside its screen with its own control: the Collider's $(thing)Beam Focus$(), the Crucible's $(thing)Plasma Temperature$(), the Omnilex's $(thing)Law Coherence$().

Day 19. The ideal setting $(thing)drifts$() while the machine runs, each machine its own way: some wander, some swing back and forth, some steadily fall, some sit still then suddenly jump. Match it to keep $(thing)efficiency$() high. The panel shows two waves; when I am close they line up and go clean, like two tuning forks falling into unison.

$(thing)Overclock$() doubles speed but quadruples power draw - a square law, like resistive heating. $(thing)Parallel$() runs several recipes per cycle. Generators cannot overclock; tuning sets their output instead.

$(thing)Containment$() wears down while running - faster when overclocked or out of tune. At zero the machine $(thing)faults$(): work in progress is lost and it stops. A $(item)Field Calibrator$() used on the controller restores it. It also reveals the ideal setting, marked in gold on the panel.

Much later: an $(item)Autonomous Calibrator$() can be installed into a controller. From then on the machine follows its own drift and repairs itself, for a 25% power tax and 10% less generator output. Worth every joule.$(br2)Pack makers can slow or disable drift and wear in the config.
Even empty space jitters. This machine $(thing)generates power$() from vacuum fluctuations, burning Casimir plates and exotic matter as catalysts.$(br2)$(thing)Tier 1$() machine.

Honest note: textbook physics says the vacuum's ground state cannot be mined - there is nothing lower to fall to. But the Casimir effect is real: plates set close together feel a measurable push. The $(item)Zero-Point Energy Extractor$() leans on that, with Casimir plates and exotic matter as catalysts. And it does generate power.
